title: Thumpkin and the Bell of Laughter
markdown:
Thumpkin had planned a day with no rescues in it. No prophecies. Quiet, among the whispering peaks, and nettle tea at the proper strength. He was a large ogre — hands that could cradle a boulder like a cup, footsteps that told the snowdrifts someone substantial was passing — and he kept a library of delicate poetry and a fondness for hours that did not knock. Clover, his mountain goat, shared the preference. She cropped alpine herbs by the stone cottage, wool dusted with pollen, eyes that missed very little.

“Imagine it,” he had rumbled that morning, watching sun find the snow-caps. “No visitors. No gnome mittens. Sky, and a cloud worth looking at.” Clover maaed and rolled a pebble with her nose. That was the shape of the day they wanted.

Mountain magic, as it turned out, did not consult the tea diary.

A sleek black cat arrived from the air and landed as if a schedule had been waiting. Fur drank the light. Emerald eyes conducted an interview. This was Professor Paws, and he wore the manner of someone who had hired you and found you late. Whiskers ticked.

“About time,” he said, a deep purr with a clipboard in it. “The retrieval window is closing. The mountain’s equilibrium is at stake.”

Thumpkin blinked. Clover cocked an ear. “Retrieval window? I think you have the wrong cottage. I am Thumpkin. This is Clover. We were hoping for quiet.”

A tail-flick that could have cut glass. “The contract is clear. Large capable individual. Delicate retrieval. Unspecified item, high importance. Payment: premium salmon pâté, thrice weekly, for life. Are we going? My patience is finite. Quiet sounds dull.”

Thumpkin felt a smile arrive without permission. Being hired by a cat was not quiet. Duty, however, had always been larger than his objections, and pâté had a way of sounding like a reason. Clover appeared to be computing the same equation.

“Salmon pâté. Where is the item? My joints prefer a warm-up.”

Professor Paws was already on the goat track, tail a banner. “Keep up. Lagging reflects on my hiring. Clover — you have sense. Pace.”

The quiet day went like mist. Thumpkin’s careful boom of a walk made the ground consider him; Clover’s hooves found the old holds as if the mountain had left them labelled. They followed the cat along paths where distant mule bells travelled on cold wind, a thin music that made the satchel’s thermos clink in answer. Heather gave way to stone. Stone gave way to a ledge that enjoyed drama. Professor Paws did not look back except to measure their lateness.

“Not a picnic,” he said, when Thumpkin paused to admire a lenticular cloud that would have been the whole afternoon, once. “Equilibrium, Ogre. Keep the joints moving.”

Light gathered on snow until the world looked silvered and privately theatrical. Their shadows went long and polite. A hare watched from a distance that suggested it had heard about pâté and remained unmoved. Clover snatched a mouthful of something tough and alpine; Paws sighed as if vegetation were a breach of contract.

A chasm asked for a log. Thumpkin crossed it the way a glacier crosses a century, wood complaining, weight placed as if it had been rehearsed. Clover hopped it like a garden fence, her own small bell pleased with itself. Beyond, a marmot guarded a patch of ruby berries, chest puffed, whiskers on duty.

“Halt. Tribute. Prize berries. I guard them with everything I have.”

Professor Paws narrowed his fire-green look. “The ogre requires passage. Your berries are irrelevant. Step aside, rodent.”

The marmot was not used to irrelevance, or to the word rodent. It stamped. Thumpkin reached into the satchel that usually held verse and a thermos and brought out a pine bird he had carved for himself, smooth, fragrant. “Perhaps this. It sings if you hold it to the wind.”

The marmot’s eyes took the moonlight, snatched the bird, tested a squeak, and left enchanted, berries forgotten. Thumpkin murmured to Clover, “Giving travels further than shouting.” She bleated as if she had known and nudged his hand.

They climbed until Thumpkin’s knees filed a complaint and then, being ogre knees, continued. Professor Paws communicated mostly in tail and in the particular silence of a cat who has already decided you are trying. Cryptic lefts. A right that was only a right if you were four-footed and vain. Clover translated the worst of it by going first.

After an age of those flicks and disdainful sighs they came to a gorge that roared as if it had been waiting to be the setting. A waterfall sheeted the cliff; moonlight made a curtain of it, water becoming something you could almost read. The sound lived in the ribs. Spray salted the air. On a moss ledge behind the shimmer, tucked where a sensible person would not put valuables, sat the reason.

“The Bell of Echoed Laughter,” Professor Paws said. “Misplaced. An oversight. Retrieve it.”

Thumpkin measured the drop and his own width and shook his head. Clover, though — Clover could stand on places that made other goats write letters home.

“If I steady you,” he said, voice an anchor under the roar, “you could nudge it.”

She butted his palm. He made a platform of one enormous hand. She hopped up. He lifted, slow, as if the air might bruise. Clover’s hooves found damp moss; her bell gave a brave note; her nose sent the silver thing tumbling. It landed at his feet with a ting: tarnished, carved with smiling faces, a faint joyous echo that tickled the ear like a joke told in another valley.

Professor Paws produced a satisfied motor of a purr. “Excellent, operative. Pâté tomorrow. Worthy.”

The way back was easier and almost companionable. The professor permitted Clover a brief rub against his dark fur. In a sheltered valley the lights of Hearthstone came on like a careful constellation. Word of the bell had walked faster than they had.

The square held no fanfare and no podium. Tables had been dragged out as if someone had remembered hospitality at the last useful minute: crusty bread still warm in the crumb, stew that smelled of rosemary and thyme, jars of berry jam catching lamplight and looking briefly like smaller, tamer waterfalls. Children ran with laughter that needed no silverware. A woman pressed a bowl into Thumpkin’s hands without asking him to make a speech about retrieval windows. An old man tapped the bell once, experimentally, and grinned when it answered with someone else’s chuckle.

Thumpkin sat by a crackling fire, pleased in a quiet way that did not require an audience. Clover dozed on his boots, pollen still in the wool, the day’s un-taken cloud forgotten. Professor Paws accepted a saucer of the richest cream with a nod that said the village had, for once, met a standard. The Bell of Echoed Laughter, on a worn velvet cushion, chimed when someone told a story that had a grin in it, and otherwise kept still, which Thumpkin respected.

No one asked him to explain the mountains. He poured imaginary nettle tea in his mind, tasted the real stew, and watched Paws pretend not to enjoy the cream. The pâté, he suspected, would arrive whether or not the day had been the one he ordered. He would shelve the poetry again tomorrow. Tonight the fire popped, the mule bells on the ridge had gone to bed, and Clover’s small bell, under her chin, ticked once in a dream.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
